title: Use of OSI IS-IS for Routing in TCP/IP and Dual Environments
summary: Specifies an integrated routing protocol, based on OSI IS-IS, that can serve as an interior gateway protocol for TCP/IP, OSI, or mixed networks. This lets one routing protocol handle both kinds of traffic. It was developed by the IETF IS-IS working group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1195 extends the IS-IS routing protocol so routers can exchange routes for IP, OSI, or both. It adds IP addresses and reachability data to IS-IS messages while keeping one shared hierarchy of areas. The design avoids operating two fully separate routing protocols in a mixed network.

questions: what is the difference between level 1 and level 2 is-is
what is ships in the night routing
how does is-is carry ip routes
subtitle: One link-state routing protocol for IP, OSI, or networks carrying both kinds of traffic.

tldr.problem: Networks carrying both TCP/IP and OSI traffic could run two separate routing protocols, which duplicated work and configuration. RFC 1195 defines an integrated alternative based on OSI IS-IS.
tldr.mechanism: Integrated IS-IS adds IP reachability and interface information to existing IS-IS packets. Routers share a two-level area hierarchy and calculate routes using link-state information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1195 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 1349, RFC 5302 and RFC 5304. The authentication mechanism it defines is a clear-text password, described as weak protection against accidental configuration errors.

today: RFC 1195 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 1349, RFC 5302 and RFC 5304. Its text describes the proposal as based on the then-current OSI IS-IS draft and expects later versions to track the final International Standard.

sections.title: One Routing Protocol for IP and OSI
sections.content:
RFC 1195 extends the OSI Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) routing protocol to support TCP/IP as well as OSI. It is an interior gateway protocol, which means it calculates routes inside one routing domain. Routers forward IP and OSI packets directly over their link-layer services; the protocol does not wrap one type inside the other.

The RFC contrasts this design with “Ships in the Night,” where a router runs independent routing protocols for each suite. Integrated IS-IS supports IP-only, OSI-only and dual routers, while carrying the routing information in a common protocol. It relies on the link-state Shortest Path First algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Integrated IS-IS lets routers use one routing protocol to exchange routes for IP and OSI traffic. A router can support IP, OSI, or both, and the packets themselves remain separate on the network links.

sections.title: Areas and the Two Routing Levels
sections.content:
IS-IS divides a routing domain into areas and uses two levels. A level 1 router knows routes within its area and sends traffic for elsewhere to a nearby level 2 router. Level 2 routers exchange routes between areas and must form a connected backbone; the RFC provides no way to repair a partition of that backbone using level 1 links.

Integrated IS-IS applies the same hierarchy to IP and OSI. Each area is IP-only, OSI-only or dual, and the design does not permit partially overlapping IP and OSI areas or separate backbones. A dual area contains dual routers only; if both kinds of traffic must cross areas, all level 2 routers must be dual.
sections.plainLanguage: Level 1 routers handle destinations inside their area, while level 2 routers connect areas. The same levels carry both kinds of routes, but the RFC sets rules about which router types can share an area or connect the areas.

sections.title: Advertising and Choosing IP Routes
sections.content:
Level 1 link-state packets list IP address, subnet mask and metric entries that a router can reach. If an IP destination matches an entry in the area, the router uses level 1 routing; otherwise it sends the packet toward a level 2 router. When several entries match, the more specific subnet mask wins. Level 2 routers advertise routes between areas and may summarize several area routes with manually configured entries.

Route selection prefers a reachable route inside the area over a level 2 route. At level 2, internal metrics take precedence over external metrics; routers then consider the best address match, requested Type of Service metric support and path cost. Optional metrics include delay, expense and error, alongside the default metric. A default route is allowed only as an external level 2 route, and the RFC warns that it can create black holes.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise the IP networks they can reach, with a mask and a cost for each route. They prefer a more specific matching route, routes inside the area, and then the shortest suitable path.

sections.title: Sharing Information Between Routers
sections.content:
IS-IS packets carry variable-length fields encoded as code, length and value. The code and length each take one octet, and the value can be up to 254 octets. Routers must ignore and pass through codes they do not recognize, allowing IP-only routers to ignore OSI-specific fields and OSI-only routers to ignore IP-specific fields.

IP-capable routers advertise supported network protocols, their interface addresses in Hello packets, and reachable IP prefixes in link-state packets. A Hello may list up to 63 IP addresses for an interface. Reachability entries are 12 octets and include metric information, an IP address and a subnet mask. Level 2 packets can also carry external route information for border routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers add labeled fields to IS-IS messages to announce which protocols and IP networks they support. Routers that do not understand a field can pass it along without using it.

sections.title: IS-IS Addresses for IP-Only Routers
sections.content:
IS-IS packet formats require every router to have an OSI-style Network Service Access Point (NSAP) address, even if the router handles only IP. The address is used by IS-IS, not as an address for the router's other IP protocols. The RFC recommends obtaining a normal NSAP address, including in an IP-only network, because it simplifies a possible move to dual operation.

If a normal assignment is not wanted, an IP-only router can derive a compatible address from its autonomous-system number, area and router identifier. The RFC describes an address format with AFI 47, ICD 00 05, reserved bytes 00 00 and fields for the routing domain, area, identifier and selector. Routers in one area must share the same high-order area portion.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS requires each router to have an OSI-style address, even when the router carries only IP traffic. The RFC recommends a normal assignment or describes how an IP-only router can form an address for IS-IS use.

sections.title: New Fields in IS-IS Packets
sections.content:
The existing IS-IS packet types and fixed fields stay in place. RFC 1195 adds variable-length fields for protocols supported (code 129), IP internal reachability (128), IP external reachability (130), inter-domain routing information (131), IP interface addresses (132) and authentication (133).

The protocols-supported field appears in all Hellos and in link-state packet number 0 from IP-capable routers. Reachability entries use code-length-value encoding and cannot appear in pseudonode link-state packets. The RFC also corrects the encoding of variable fields in sequence-number packets so the IP fields can be carried there.
sections.plainLanguage: Integrated IS-IS keeps the established packet types and adds fields for IP routes, interface addresses, supported protocols and authentication. The code and length fields let older or unrelated routers skip information they do not use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IS-IS packets may include authentication information, and the field can support different mechanisms. RFC 1195 defines only a simple password sent in clear text without encryption. A packet with invalid authentication is discarded, and split link-state or sequence-number packets are authenticated independently.

The RFC says the password provides no useful protection against intentional misbehavior. It describes it instead as weak protection against accidental errors such as misconfiguration. Other authentication mechanisms and other security topics are outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The only authentication method defined here sends a password without encryption. The RFC says it may catch accidental mistakes but does not protect against deliberate interference.
